message.content:
CONTEXT: You are reverse-engineering a compiled C++ "inflection" library (Rails-style Inflector) purely as a black box.
BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test11_executable   (run from any cwd; it needs no files)
USAGE: ./test11_executable <int num> <word>    -- requires argc > 2, then prints exactly 11 lines.
LINE MAP (1-indexed):
  1  pluralize(word)
  2  ordinalize(num)
  3  camelize(word, true)
  4  camelize(word, false)
  5  titleize(word)
  6  capitalize(word)
  7  truncate(word, 5)
  8  truncate(word, 10, "~")
  9  parameterize(word)
  10 parameterize(word, "_")
  11 isPlural(word)  -> prints 0 or 1
HOW TO PROBE ONE LINE:
  /workspace/dataset/test11_executable 1 'my_word' | sed -n '3p'
Use single quotes or printf to control argv exactly. To probe words containing spaces, quotes, newlines, backslashes, or
non-ASCII UTF-8, pass them as a SINGLE argv element (e.g. "$(printf 'a\tb')" or 'héllo'). Empty word: '' (still argc>2).

ALREADY ESTABLISHED — treat as given, do NOT spend probes re-deriving:
  * pluralize(w) = w + "s", UNLESS w exactly (case-sensitively) equals one of the uncountables
      {equipment, information, rice, money, species, series, fish, sheep, jeans, police}  -> then w unchanged.
      (The library's 17 plural regex rules are dead code: the first registered rule /$/ -> "s" always matches first.)
  * isPlural(w) == (singularize(w) != w).  isSingular(w) == !isPlural(w).
  * The library registers 23 singular regex rules (Rails standard) plus a first rule /s$/ -> "" ; first match wins,
    iterating in registration order. There are NO irregular() pairs and NO human() rules (person->persons, child->childs).
  * An acronyms table exists containing exactly: HTML, HTTP, XML, JSON, API.
  * Other literals in the binary: "..." (truncate default omission), "-" (parameterize default sep), "_", " ", "::",
    "_id", "id", "th", "st", "nd", "rd".
  * The C++ is compiled with gcc-12, uses std::regex (ECMAScript grammar) and std::string (byte-oriented, no UTF-8 awareness).

OPTIONAL EXTRA TOOL: you may disassemble to resolve ambiguity (objdump and nm are at /opt/compiler/gcc-12/bin/, on PATH).
  objdump -dC --start-address=0xADDR --stop-address=0xADDR2 /workspace/dataset/test11_executable
  Symbol addresses: pluralize 0x405d12, singularize 0x405f84, camelize 0x406262, underscore 0x40636e, classify 0x40649a,
  tableize 0x40650a, humanize 0x406576, titleize 0x4066fe, ordinalize 0x40681c, dasherize 0x406992, parameterize 0x406a1a,
  isPlural 0x406bc0, isSingular 0x406c0c, upcase 0x406c2a, downcase 0x406cea, capitalize 0x406daa, decapitalize 0x406ed0,
  truncate 0x406f98, demodulize 0x40705a, deconstantize 0x4070c8, foreign_key 0x40716e, ordinal 0x4071e8, initialize 0x403cd4.
  Disassembly is a tiebreaker; observed behavior is the ground truth.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT:
  * Do NOT write, create, or modify any file anywhere. Read-only + running the binary only. Never touch /output.
  * Run many probes (aim 40-80). Batch them in for-loops so it is cheap. Quote carefully.
  * Adversarially attack your own hypothesis: for every rule you state, try to find an input that breaks it.
  * The goal is a byte-exact Rust reimplementation using only std. Where behavior is byte-oriented rather than
    char-oriented (UTF-8 multibyte input), say so explicitly, because Rust's String indexing would panic there.


=== camelize ===
YOUR SLICE: camelize(word, bool) — lines 3 (bool=true) and 4 (bool=false).
Known: camelize("cat",true)=="cat", camelize("cat",false)=="Cat", so the bool appears to mean "lowercase the first letter".
Determine EXACTLY: how underscores, dashes, spaces, dots, digits, "::" / "/" path separators, leading/trailing/repeated
underscores are handled; whether the acronym table (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) is consulted (probe 'html_tag', 'api_key',
'xml', 'json_data', 'http_request', 'my_html_parser', and the same in mixed case); what happens to already-CamelCase or
UPPERCASE input; whether characters after the first are ever lowercased; empty string; word starting with a digit or
underscore or non-ASCII. Also determine whether the two bool variants differ ONLY in the first character.

attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

camelize(word: &str/&[u8], lower_first: bool) -> bytes

CONFIRMED by disassembly at 0x406262 (in-place mutation of a copy) AND by a 250-case
randomized differential test (0 mismatches). The C++ source is exactly:

  std::string camelize(const std::string& s, bool lowerFirst) {
      std::string result = s;              // byte-for-byte copy
      bool cap = !lowerFirst;              // xor 0x1  (see 0x40628f)
      size_t i = 0;
      while (i < result.size()) {          // size() re-read EVERY iteration
          if (result[i] == '_') {          // 0x5f, the ONLY special byte
              cap = true;
              result.erase(i, 1);          // delete the underscore
              i -= 1;                      // size_t; wraps if i==0, then +1 -> 0
          } else if (cap) {
              result[i] = (char)toupper((int)(signed char)result[i]);  // movsbl -> toupper
              cap = false;
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      return result;                       // trailing `cap` state is discarded
  }

Rust reimplementation (byte-oriented; do NOT use char indexing):

  fn camelize(word: &str, lower_first: bool) -> String {
      let mut b: Vec<u8> = word.as_bytes().to_vec();
      let mut cap = !lower_first;
      let mut i: usize = 0;
      while i < b.len() {
          if b[i] == b'_' {
              cap = true;
              b.remove(i);            // stay at same index i (do NOT advance)
              continue;               // equivalent to i -= 1; i += 1
          }
          if cap {
              if b[i].is_ascii_lowercase() { b[i] -= 32; }  // toupper, C locale
              cap = false;
          }
          i += 1;
      }
      // Safety: only ASCII a-z were changed to A-Z and only 0x5f bytes removed,
      // so UTF-8 validity is preserved => String::from_utf8(b).unwrap() is safe.
      String::from_utf8(b).unwrap()
  }

BEHAVIOURAL SPEC (all verified):
 1. The ONLY separator recognised is the ASCII underscore 0x5f. Every '_' is deleted
    and sets a "capitalize the next surviving byte" flag.
 2. '-', ' ', '.', '/', '::', ':', tab, newline, '~', digits, and every other byte are
    copied verbatim and do NOT trigger capitalization.
    camelize("my-word",false)=="My-word"; camelize("a/b_c",true)=="a/bC";
    camelize("a::b_c",true)=="a::bC". No '/'->'::' conversion (unlike Rails).
 3. NOTHING IS EVER LOWERCASED. There is no tolower call in the function.
    camelize("CamelCase",true)=="CamelCase"; camelize("UPPER",true)=="UPPER";
    camelize("UPPER_CASE",*)=="UPPERCASE"; camelize("FOO_bar",*)=="FOOBar".
    So `lower_first == true` does NOT mean "lowercase the first letter"; it means
    "do not uppercase the first letter".
 4. The bool only sets the INITIAL value of `cap` (cap = !lower_first). Consequences:
    - If the input's first byte is '_' (or the input is empty, or consists only of
      '_'), the two variants produce BYTE-IDENTICAL output, because the leading '_'
      sets cap=true regardless. camelize("_leading",true)==camelize("_leading",false)
      =="Leading".
    - Otherwise the two variants differ in AT MOST the first byte of the result, and
      only when that byte is ASCII a-z. All later bytes are identical in both variants
      (after the first non-'_' byte, cap is false in both paths).
 5. Leading underscores: consumed, next byte uppercased. "_a"->"A", "__double__"->"Double".
    Trailing underscores: simply deleted, cap flag left dangling and discarded.
    "a_"->"a"/"A", "ab_cd_"->"abCd"/"AbCd".
    Repeated internal underscores collapse: "a__b"->"aB"/"AB", "x__y__z"->"xYZ"/"XYZ".
    All-underscore input ("_", "__", "___") -> "" for both bools.
 6. Empty input -> "" for both bools.
 7. If the byte after an underscore is not an ASCII lowercase letter, it is emitted
    unchanged (toupper is identity) and cap is still cleared:
    "a_1b"->"a1b"/"A1b", "_9x"->"9x", "9_a"->"9A", "a_B"->"aB"/"AB",
    "_-x"->"-x", "_ x"->" x", "_\t"->"\t".
 8. THE ACRONYM TABLE (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) IS **NOT** CONSULTED. camelize is a
    pure byte loop with no table lookup, no regex, no acronym handling:
      html_tag      -> htmlTag      / HtmlTag
      api_key       -> apiKey       / ApiKey
      xml           -> xml          / Xml
      json_data     -> jsonData     / JsonData
      http_request  -> httpRequest  / HttpRequest
      my_html_parser-> myHtmlParser / MyHtmlParser
      HTML_tag      -> HTMLTag      / HTMLTag   (preserved only because input was upper)
      Html_tag      -> HtmlTag      / HtmlTag
      HTML/JSON/API -> unchanged for both bools
      API_KEY       -> APIKEY       / APIKEY
 9. Non-ASCII / multibyte UTF-8: purely byte-oriented. toupper is called with the byte
    SIGN-EXTENDED (movsbl), i.e. a negative int for bytes >= 0x80; under the C locale
    (the program never calls setlocale — no setlocale symbol in the binary) this is
    identity for all bytes 0x80..0xFF. Verified: "_élan"->"élan" (0xC3 unchanged),
    "Ünder_score"->"ÜnderScore", "ß_x"->"ßX", "a_émile"->"aémile"/"Aémile",
    raw "_\xe9x"->"\xe9x", "_\xff"->"\xff", "_\xd0\xb0"->"\xd0\xb0".
    Locale is irrelevant: LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8 with "i_i" still yields "iI"/"II"
    (dotted-I is NOT produced), so plain ASCII a-z => A-Z mapping is correct.
10. Invalid UTF-8 / lone continuation bytes pass through untouched; only 0x5f is
    removed, so a Rust implementation over &[u8] is exactly equivalent.
11. No NUL byte can be tested (argv is NUL-terminated); assume it would be an ordinary
    byte, but a Rust &str cannot contain issues here anyway.
gotchas: lower_first=true does NOT lowercase anything. It merely skips the initial uppercasing. camelize("CamelCase", true) == "CamelCase", NOT "camelCase". Do not call to_lowercase on the first char.
The acronym table (HTML HTTP XML JSON API) is NOT used by camelize at all. Do not add acronym special-casing — html_tag must yield htmlTag/HtmlTag.

Byte-oriented, not char-oriented. Never index a Rust String/str by byte offset and slice-assign; operate on Vec<u8> (or as_bytes().to_vec()) and only mutate ASCII a-z -> A-Z. Naive `s.chars()` + `to_uppercase()` breaks on multibyte input: 'é' after '_' must stay 'é' (0xC3 0xA9), not become 'É'.

toupper is called with a SIGN-EXTENDED char (movsbl) so bytes >= 0x80 arrive as negative ints; in the C locale glibc returns them unchanged. Using char::to_ascii_uppercase on the byte reproduces this; using Unicode uppercasing does not.
No setlocale is ever called, so the mapping is fixed ASCII a-z -> A-Z regardless of LC_ALL. Verified with LC_ALL=tr_TR.UTF-8: 'i_i' -> 'iI'/'II'.
Only 0x5f ('_') is a separator. Dashes, spaces, dots, '/', '::' are NOT. Rails' camelize converts '/' to '::' — this implementation does not.

The erase-and-step-back loop uses `i -= 1` on a size_t; when i == 0 this wraps to SIZE_MAX and the following `i += 1` brings it back to 0. In Rust use `b.remove(i); continue;` (no decrement) — a literal `i -= 1` would panic on underflow in debug builds.
size() is re-evaluated each iteration, so the loop correctly shrinks as underscores are erased. Caching the length would read past the end.
Trailing underscores leave the capitalize flag set, but it is discarded — do not append or capitalize anything at the end. "a_" -> "a" / "A".
Empty input and all-underscore input return the empty string for BOTH bool values; the two variants are identical there (and whenever the first byte is '_').
Characters after the first surviving character are never case-changed unless immediately preceded by an underscore. "ZZ_zz" -> "ZZZz" for both bools.
The two bool variants can differ ONLY in the first byte of the result (and only when the input does not start with '_' and that byte is ASCII a-z). Don't assume a general-case transform between them.

Invalid UTF-8 in the input passes through byte-for-byte (only 0x5f is dropped), so an implementation over &str is fine only because the removed/changed bytes are ASCII; prefer Vec<u8> internally and unwrap from_utf8 (guaranteed valid).
unresolved: Behavior with an embedded NUL byte (0x00) cannot be probed because argv strings are NUL-terminated. By inspection of the disassembly it would be treated as an ordinary non-'_' byte (toupper(0)==0), but this is unverified.
Whether camelize is invoked internally by other exposed functions with a different bool (e.g. classify/titleize paths) was out of scope for this slice; only lines 3 and 4 were probed.
